title: The Company That Invented the Digital Camera... and Buried It
description: In 1975 a 24-year-old Kodak engineer built the first digital camera. His bosses told him to keep it quiet. Thirty-seven years later, Kodak was bankrupt. This is the story of the most expensive mistake in the history of photography.
notes: FACT-CHECK before recording: Kodak market share (~90% film, mid-70s estimate), the 'cute, don't tell anyone' quote (Sasson's own recollection), 1981 internal study, Instagram headcount/price, Kodak peak headcount.

scenes.text: In nineteen seventy-five, a twenty-four-year-old engineer carried a strange machine into a conference room at Kodak, and showed his bosses the future of photography. They watched. And one of them said: "That's cute. But don't tell anyone about it." Thirty-seven years later, Kodak went bankrupt. And the thing they told him to hide... is the reason why.

This is the story of the most expensive mistake in the history of photography. And here is what makes it terrifying: nobody at Kodak was stupid. Every single decision made perfect sense. Right up until the end.

To understand how big Kodak was, picture America in nineteen seventy-five. By most estimates, about nine out of every ten rolls of film sold there came in a little yellow box. Weddings, birthdays, summer holidays. If it was remembered, it probably passed through Kodak.

And the business model was a work of genius. Founder George Eastman had worked it out decades earlier: sell the camera cheap, barely above cost. Then make a fortune selling the film, again and again, forever. Kodak wasn't really a camera company. It was a film company.

Now meet Steven Sasson. Fresh out of school, newly hired as an electrical engineer at Kodak's lab in Rochester. His boss gave him a vague, almost casual task: find out whether a new invention called a CCD chip could be used to capture images.

No big budget. No team. A workbench, a lone technician, and a pile of spare parts. Nobody had ever built what he was attempting. So he scavenged. A movie camera lens. A cassette tape recorder. Batteries. Wires. A lot of wires.

After about a year, he had it. A machine the size of a toaster, weighing about eight pounds. It captured a black-and-white image, one hundred pixels wide and one hundred tall, and stored it on a cassette tape. Your phone takes photos with more than a thousand times that detail. And it needed twenty-three seconds to record just one.

But then the image appeared on a television screen. Grainy. Blurry. Beautiful. A photograph, with no film, no chemicals, and no darkroom. Sasson knew he was holding something that had never existed before.
So he carried it into that conference room full of executives, and demonstrated it. Light in. Cassette tape. Television out. He expected excitement. He got confusion.
They asked him: why would anyone want to look at photographs on a television? And then came the sentence he would remember for the rest of his life. "That's cute. But don't tell anyone about it."

Here's the thing. They weren't irrational. A camera that needs no film is a direct threat to a company that makes its fortune selling film. For Kodak, Sasson hadn't brought them an invention. He'd brought them a very polite funeral invitation.
But the story gets stranger. Because Kodak didn't ignore the idea. They did something worse.

They locked it down. Kodak patented the technology, and then kept the idea on a shelf. Years later, an internal study warned that digital photography would likely overtake film, and urged the company to prepare. The company kept its eyes on film.

Meanwhile, the world kept moving. In nineteen eighty-one, Sony showed off an electronic camera that needed no film at all. In the years after, Japanese rivals like Fuji and Canon quietly built digital machines. The door Kodak had opened was now being walked through by everyone else.

Kodak did eventually go digital. And it was good at it. In the early two-thousands, Kodak was among the best-selling digital camera brands in America. But now it had walked into a trap of its own making. Every digital camera sold meant fewer rolls of film sold. And film was where the profit lived. Kodak was competing against itself.
Then film sales fell off a cliff. Phones began carrying cameras. What Kodak had treated as a side project became the entire business overnight, and Kodak had no wall left to hide behind.

On January nineteenth, two thousand twelve, Kodak, the company that had invented the modern snapshot, filed for bankruptcy protection. A company that once employed well over a hundred thousand people.

And here's the part that still stings. Less than three months later, a tiny photo-sharing app called Instagram was sold to Facebook for one billion dollars. How many employees did it have? Thirteen. Thirteen people, against a hundred thousand.

And Steven Sasson? He spent decades at Kodak. And he was later awarded the National Medal of Technology and Innovation, one of America's highest honors for technological achievement. For inventing the exact thing his company asked him to hide.

scenes.text: So the lesson isn't that Kodak was foolish. They had the invention. The patent. The talent. The money. Even the warning. What they lacked was the courage to disrupt themselves before someone else did.

Remember that sentence from the beginning. "That's cute. But don't tell anyone about it." The most dangerous words in business aren't "this will never work." They are "this works... and we would rather not know."
Next time: on the very same day, in the very same city, two men raced to patent the telephone. Hours apart. One became a legend. The other was almost erased from history. Do you know his name?
